messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulation issues
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet List,

I'm finally embarking on a simulation study of the statistical properties
of ERGMs as implemented in statnet. I'm setting up the code to run these
simulations, but as I did so, I noted some strange things.

I simulated (sparse) networks of 100 nodes, with an edge parameter of -6.
Fitting a model with only edges to this worked fine (estimates fell around
the true value), but when I fitted a model that also included triangles,
estimates of the triangle parameter followed a bimodal distribution;
57/100 simulations had triangle estimates of -12 to -13 (so, effectively
zero on the antilog scale), whereas 43/100 simulations had triangle
parameters greater than 0. In addition, the LRT test statistic between the
null and the alternative model was larger than I expected:

> sum(unlist(lldiff)*2>3.84)
[1] 16
> summary(unlist(lldiff)*2)
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
 0.005212  1.253000  2.704000  3.217000  3.429000 26.660000

Has anyone had any similar experiences with simulated data?

Thanks
Simon

messages.body_plain:
sdfrost@ucsd.edu wrote:
> Dear Statnet List,
> 
> I'm finally embarking on a simulation study of the statistical properties
> of ERGMs as implemented in statnet. I'm setting up the code to run these
> simulations, but as I did so, I noted some strange things.
> 
> I simulated (sparse) networks of 100 nodes, with an edge parameter of -6.
> Fitting a model with only edges to this worked fine (estimates fell around
> the true value), but when I fitted a model that also included triangles,
> estimates of the triangle parameter followed a bimodal distribution;
> 57/100 simulations had triangle estimates of -12 to -13 (so, effectively
> zero on the antilog scale), whereas 43/100 simulations had triangle
> parameters greater than 0. In addition, the LRT test statistic between the
> null and the alternative model was larger than I expected:
> 
>> sum(unlist(lldiff)*2>3.84)
> [1] 16
>> summary(unlist(lldiff)*2)
>      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
>  0.005212  1.253000  2.704000  3.217000  3.429000 26.660000
> 
> Has anyone had any similar experiences with simulated data?
> 

The former is a known phenomenon (at least, if I understand your setup 
correctly).  It is easiest to describe using some simple notation: let G 
be the random graph whose distribution is the ERG defined by parameter 
vector theta and sufficient statistic vector t.  (I'll ignore the 
support for now, since it's mostly irrelevant...take the support of G to 
be all graphs on N vertices, if you like.)  Now, define the mean value 
parameter, tau, as follows:

tau(theta) = E(t(G)|theta)

where E(a|b) is the conditional expectation of a given b.  Clearly, for 
any choice of theta and t on a fixed support, there will be one value of 
tau; what's not so obvious (but true, nonetheless) is that every 
realizable value of tau corresponds to one value of theta.  That is, 
there's a 1:1 mapping between the vector of mean values of the 
sufficient statistics, and the vector of model parameters.

This observation sometimes leads to the misapprehension that the 
distribution of t(G) (here, the edge and triangle counts) will be 
concentrated about tau(theta).  As you have observed, this is not the 
case -- it is possible to get multimodal distributions for t(G) which do 
not cluster tightly about the mean.  In fact, things are worse than 
that: there is no guarantee that _any_ substantial probability mass will 
be found near the tau(theta)!  This is quite striking in the case of the 
MLE, since (for regular families, at least), the MLE satisfies the relation

tau(thetahat) = t(G_obs)

where thetahat is the MLE of theta, and G_obs is the observed network. 
The MLE, then, effectively sets the expected statistics equal to the 
observed statistics under the model (assuming the MLE exists, of 
course).  This is a very nice feature, but is not quite so beneficent as 
it might appear; this is because the model can "cheat," by producing a 
distribution whose mean matches the data, but which nearly always 
generates graphs whose properties are unlike the observed graph.  This 
has been studied extensively by Mark Handcock, who has looked in detail 
at some of the properties which lead models to produce this sort of 
behavior.  It's well worth looking at his work on model degeneracy, if 
you want additional details.

Anyway, what does this have to do with your case?  If I correctly 
understand your strategy, you are taking a model with parameter theta, 
simulating draws from it, and then finding the MLEs for the simulated 
networks.  From the above, it is quite possible that your model produces 
a bimodal distribution of triangle/edge count vectors (triangle terms 
are infamous for this).  Fitting the model to this bimodal graph 
distribution is likely to generate a bimodal distribution of MLEs, whose 
  modes correspond to the modes of the distribution of input statistics. 
  It is also likely that you will get some simulated networks whose 
statistics are on the boundary of the convex hull of possible 
statistics.  In that case, the MLE won't exist at all for some draws.  I 
would also note that some granularity may be expected in the MLE 
distribution when on the edge of the convex hull (especially for small 
graphs), because the "jump" from an expectation of, say, 1 triangle to 
an expectation of 2 triangles may involve a larger shift in the 
parameter space than the jump from 100 triangles to 101 triangles. 
IIRC, Mark has also looked at this, although I can't recall exactly what 
was found.

Hopefully, that helps shed some light on the phenomenon.  Mark and the 
others should certainly chime in if I've mischaracterized the State 'O 
Knowledge on the matter....

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Simulation issues - the curse of degeneracy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon, I'll add a little to Carter's great response.  Yes, it sounds to 
me like you're running into the classic degeneracy problem, as Carter 
pointed out.  In my own simulations I've found that the triangle 
parameterization almost always leads to degeneracy in anything but the 
smallest of networks.  Mark Handcock's book chapter and working paper on 
degeneracy are the places to start for a deeper understanding (to find 
them, searching on Handcock and degeneracy in Google Scholar should get 
you to everything).

It is precisely this problem that led to the development of new 
parameterizations for network statistics that can capture triangle closure 
and other dyadic-depedent processes, but in a non-degenerate way.  These 
are explained in an article by Snijders et al that just came out in 
Sociological Meythodology.  Hunter and Handcock have a Penn State 
Statistics working paper that further develops them, and then there's a 
special issue of Social Networks coming out with a cluster of papers that 
explains and applies them to some examples.  So no shortage of stuff to 
read on the topic - just very little that's already appeared in the 
literature, unfortunately!

Most of the relevant unpublished articles appear as working papers either 
at UW, Penn State, Melbourne, or Gronigen.  Which suggests to me that we 
really should have an up-to-date page that links to all of them from the 
Statnet webpage.

Hope that helps,
Steve
